title: Sorrify the easy branches and work the hardest case first
intent: Order a multi-case proof so that the recognisably hardest branch is attempted first while the easy branches are stubbed with `sorry`, so that if the hard case cannot be proved, the effort already spent on the easy cases is not wasted.

children.name: case n = 0
children.closed_by: sorry (deferred by the rule; comment '-- fill in later')

children.name: case n = 1
children.closed_by: sorry (deferred by the rule; comment '-- fill in later')

children.name: case n + 2
children.closed_by: left open and worked first (comment '-- WORK ON THIS FIRST'; no sorry)

applicability.goal_shape: A Lean goal whose proof proceeds by a `match` or case split with several branches, exactly one of which is recognisably the hard case (typically the recursive/structural case `n + 2` set against easy base cases `0`, `1`).
applicability.use_when: one branch is clearly harder than the rest and you want to discover as early as possible whether the whole proof is feasible; place `sorry` on the easy branches and prove the hard branch first.
applicability.avoid_when: all branches are about equally hard, or all easy (the ordering then saves nothing); the 'hard' branch is not in fact the risk, e.g. the easy branches carry the only subtle content; or you already know the proof works and just need every branch filled, since the skill's own Verification rule forbids leaving any `sorry` in a completed proof.

claims.claim: In the example match, exactly the two base cases carry `sorry` — `| 0 => sorry -- fill in later` (line 52) and `| 1 => sorry -- fill in later` (line 53) — while the recursive case `| n + 2 => -- WORK ON THIS FIRST` (line 54) carries no `sorry`, only the comment `-- WORK ON THIS FIRST`.

The skill states the rule and its reason in its own words: 'When a proof has multiple cases, `sorry` the easy cases and work on the hardest one first. If the hard case fails, effort on easy cases is wasted.' (line 48).

Two of the three branches of the example match are sorrified (carry `sorry`) and one is left open; the two sorrified branches are the base cases 0 and 1, and the single open branch is the recursive case n + 2.
claims.evidence: count of `sorry` tokens over lines 50-55 of the copied file: 2 `sorry` across 3 branches (lines 52-53), the third branch (line 54) has none

claims.claim: The same file's Verification rule bounds the move, requiring the temporary holes to be closed before the proof counts as done: 'Never declare a proof complete while `sorry` placeholders or error diagnostics remain.' (line 93).

metrics.how_counted: counted over the example match at lines 51-54 of the copied file: two branches `| 0 => sorry` (52) and `| 1 => sorry` (53) carry `sorry`; the branch `| n + 2` (54) carries no `sorry`, only the comment `-- WORK ON THIS FIRST`

consequences: Leaves `sorry` holes on the easy branches that must be filled later; Lean accepts `sorry` as an axiom, so the theorem type-checks while those branches are open. The `match` must still be exhaustive over `n` (the base cases `0`, `1` plus the recursive case `n + 2` cover all naturals). The move is a scheduling heuristic, not a reduction: it makes no branch smaller, it only front-loads the one most likely to kill the proof. Failure mode: misjudging which branch is hard defers the risky work instead of surfacing it, and the skill's own Verification rule (line 93) forbids leaving the deferred `sorry`s in a completed proof.
